ingredients.name: water
ingredients.prep_note: as needed for moistening and the steamer

steps.title: Form granules
steps.instruction: Sprinkle water gradually over the maize flour, rubbing it into fine, loose granules. Do not make a batter.

steps.title: Prepare the steamer
steps.instruction: Bring water to a boil below a couscous steamer. Line its upper basket with a clean, light steaming cloth and add the maize. Keep the maize above the water.

steps.title: First steaming
steps.instruction: Cover and steam for about 30 minutes. Transfer carefully to a bowl, loosen with a spoon and let it cool enough to handle.

steps.title: Moisten and loosen
steps.instruction: Sprinkle with a little water and salt to taste. Rest for 10 minutes, then separate the granules. Replenish the steamer water as needed.

steps.title: Steam again
steps.instruction: Steam for another 30 minutes, until soft. If still firm, loosen and steam for up to 15 minutes more, checking the water below.

steps.title: Serve
steps.instruction: Fluff the maize and serve with ready-made cultured milk. Add sugar or salt to taste.

recipes.name: Oleleh
recipes.description: A vegetarian Oleleh adaptation: black-eyed bean pudding cooked by covered water-bath steaming.
recipes.story: Based on Isata’s vegetarian preparation published by Healthy Living Platform. It uses vegetables instead of fish.
recipes.occasion: Serve as a savoury snack or alongside a meal.
recipes.regional_variations: Pamela Greene’s Sierra Leone recipe uses fish and palm oil and steams portions in wrappers or containers.
recipes.review_summary: Replaces the generic frying template with a named cook’s steamed vegetarian version. Active preparation estimate excludes overnight soaking; doneness governs cooking time. Nutrition has not been calculated for this version.

ingredients.name: water
ingredients.prep_note: for blending; additional water for soaking and the water bath

steps.title: Prepare beans
steps.instruction: Soak the dried beans overnight, then drain and remove their skins.

steps.title: Blend
steps.instruction: Blend beans with water, onion, garlic, salt, oil and half of each pepper until smooth.

steps.title: Add vegetables
steps.instruction: Finely chop the remaining peppers and mix them into the batter with the carrot.

steps.title: Prepare water bath
steps.instruction: Heat the fan oven to 200°C. Fill greased small baking containers with batter, cover with foil and stand them in a larger tray of water.

steps.title: Steam
steps.instruction: Cook for about 40 minutes, until firm and a testing knife comes out clean.

steps.title: Serve
steps.instruction: Lift containers carefully from the hot water and serve warm.

recipes.name: Kunu Zaki
recipes.description: Kunu Zaki is a Nigeria drink built around millet or sorghum, ginger, cloves, and sweet potato, and the serving logic of cold with snacks.
recipes.story: Kunu Zaki fills a real AfroKitchen gap for Nigeria, where everyday cooking, celebration plates, street snacks, and local drinks often rely on ingredients that do not show up in generic African recipe lists. This version keeps the method practical while preserving the dish's core identity: millet or sorghum, ginger, cloves, and sweet potato, and a table built around cold with snacks.
recipes.occasion: Best for hot days, hosting, Ramadan or celebration drinks, and non-alcoholic refreshment.
recipes.regional_variations: Kunu Zaki changes by household and market availability. Cooks may adjust the main ingredient, heat level, liquid, or serving starch while keeping the same local flavor logic.
recipes.review_summary: Added in the 100-recipe gap-fill wave after comparing live AfroKitchen representation by country. The recipe keeps the most common structure for Kunu Zaki: millet or sorghum, ginger, cloves, and sweet potato, timed cooking steps, and a serving path that makes sense for Nigeria.
recommended_changes: Taste and adjust salt, chili, and acidity at the end.
Use local produce where available, and keep substitutions close to the original texture.
recipes.official_source_status: No direct ministry recipe page was found for every dish in this batch pass. The recipes are synthesized from multiple African culinary, cultural, dish-index, and beverage references, with local method patterns normalized for AfroKitchen.

steps.title: Cook or mix base
steps.instruction: Cook or whisk millet or sorghum with clean water into a smooth light base.

steps.title: Cool safely
steps.instruction: Cool until just warm so the starter is not killed.

steps.title: Ferment
steps.instruction: Stir in ginger, cloves, and sweet potato and ferment loosely covered until lightly sour.

steps.title: Serve fresh
steps.instruction: Sweeten or salt lightly, chill, and serve within a day.
